result: The authors developed a comprehensive method for long-term live imaging of leg regeneration in Parhyale hawaiensis that includes: (1) mounting and imaging under conditions that minimize photodamage while maintaining high resolution, (2) post-imaging fixation and in situ staining to identify cell fates, and (3) computer-assisted cell tracking to determine lineages.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this methodological advance. The editor states the method is 'carefully validated' and represents a 'valuable technical advance.' Reviewer 1 confirms the authors 'demonstrate the ability to image the complete leg regeneration process' and 'successfully implementing HCR in situ hybridization.' Reviewer 2 states 'the workflow...is successfully demonstrated and well documented.'

result: The authors characterize the temporal sequence of regeneration events including wound closure (scab formation, epithelial migration with little cell division), cell proliferation and morphogenesis (epithelial detachment, tissue retraction, podomere boundary formation), and differentiation (stabilization of nuclear positions). The timing varies between individuals but the order is consistent.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this characterization without challenge. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the authors 'defined three distinct phases of regeneration (wound closure, cell proliferation and morphogenesis, and differentiation) based on cellular and morphological features.' The editor notes 'the data are convincing' and 'the methodology is rigorous.'

result: The authors systematically tested imaging parameters and found that improving z-resolution enhances nuclear detection (especially in deeper layers), while improving temporal resolution enhances cell linking. The best tracking performance comes from improving both z and t resolution, though this requires more proofreading effort. Improving z-resolution alone is recommended when considering proofreading workload.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this optimization work. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'concurrently optimized imaging conditions to enable cell tracking while minimizing phototoxicity.' Reviewer 2 notes 'One movie was used to assess how imaging parameters...influence tracking reliability and the time required for manual proofreading.' The editor confirms the methodology is 'rigorous and clearly documented.'

result: The authors adapted hybridization chain reaction (HCR) for use in adult Parhyale legs, overcoming the cuticular permeability barrier that prevented conventional in situ hybridization. This method can label specific cell populations (neurons, mechanosensory organs) and can be applied after live imaging to identify tracked cells and trace their origins.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this achievement. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'successfully implementing HCR in situ hybridization in Parhyale, allowing for specific gene transcript staining at the endpoint of live imaging.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'The same sample was fixed post-imaging for in situ hybridization using an HCR protocol adapted for adult legs.' The editor notes this enables 'post-hoc in situ identification of cell types.'

result: Using the combined live imaging and HCR approach with spineless as a marker, the authors traced the origins of spineless-expressing cells in the distal carpus back to widely dispersed epidermal progenitors present at amputation. These progenitors undergo 0-2 divisions and generate mostly spineless-expressing cells.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a proof-of-principle demonstration. Reviewer 2 states 'This enabled the alignment of gene expression with specific cell lineages and the identification of progenitor cells present at the time of amputation.' However, Reviewer 2 notes 'the biological insights from the cell lineage and molecular mapping are still limited,' indicating acceptance of the result but recognition of its preliminary nature.

result: Cell tracking is most successful in the upper tissue layers (top 30 μm) with high confidence, while a smaller proportion of cells can be tracked in deeper layers due to image quality limitations.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this limitation without disputing the findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'Tracking was performed in the upper tissue layers' and notes 'Confocal microscopy was used for live imaging, which restricted imaging to the upper 30 µm tissue layer.' The editor confirms 'the data are convincing' overall.

result: Approximately 85% of animals survive the mounting and imaging procedure. Among imaged legs, 80% regenerate normally while 20% show tissue damage/retraction or arrest before regeneration onset.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these survival and success rates. Reviewer 1 states 'the data demonstrating the methodological advancement and technical feasibility are solid.' The editor confirms 'the methodology is rigorous and clearly documented.'

result: Regeneration timing varies substantially between individuals (3-10 days), with the fastest regeneration occurring in less than 3 days at 29°C. The overall speed is determined largely by variation in the early wound closure phase. Simultaneously amputated adjacent legs regenerate at similar pace, suggesting systemic factors influence regeneration speed.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this characterization. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'demonstrate the ability to image the complete leg regeneration process, spanning several days.' Reviewer 2 confirms the authors 'recorded 22 confocal time-lapse movies, starting from amputation to full regeneration.' However, Reviewer 1 notes 'much of the benchmarking and regeneration characterization remains qualitative,' suggesting acceptance but limited depth of analysis.

result: The authors added a 'backtracking' function to the Elephant tracking software that allows users to select individual cells and obtain predictions on their progenitors, particularly useful when cells of interest can be identified by molecular markers.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this software improvement as part of the overall workflow. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'employ complementary tools to analyze time-lapse movies.' The editor notes the results 'will be of interest to...advanced live imaging and cell tracking software development.'

result: Under the settings tested, deconvolution and denoising did not improve cell tracking performance.
evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute this negative finding. It is presented as part of the systematic optimization work that reviewers acknowledge as rigorous.

result: Apoptotic cells are observed during regeneration, appearing as bright pyknotic nuclei that break up and are engulfed by phagocytes. Apoptosis occurs in both imaged and non-imaged regenerating legs, indicating it is not solely due to photodamage.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations. They are presented as part of the overall characterization of regeneration that reviewers accept as convincing.

result: Light-sheet microscopy would be preferable for minimizing light exposure, but the current mounting method (gluing to coverslip) is incompatible with conventional light-sheet microscopy. The described confocal method provides the most robust approach at present.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this limitation and the authors' reasoning. Reviewer 2 states 'Light-sheet microscopy could have provided gentler imaging...While the authors acknowledge this possibility in the manuscript, they discarded it due to incompatibility between their mounting strategy and available light-sheet microscopes.' Reviewer 2 suggests 'optimizing the mounting approach for compatibility with light-sheet microscopes could enable more comprehensive tissue imaging' as a future direction, accepting the current approach as justified.

result: The authors claim Parhyale provides unique opportunities to image entire regeneration at single-cell resolution, identify progenitors and their behaviors, compare regeneration with development, and potentially describe cell lineages for every regenerated cell type when combined with appropriate markers.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the potential but note limitations. Reviewer 1 states the advances 'will serve as a useful resource' but notes 'much of the benchmarking and regeneration characterization remains qualitative' which 'limits the study's broader appeal.' Reviewer 2 states 'the methodology offers significant potential' but 'the biological insights from the cell lineage and molecular mapping are still limited.' These are forward-looking claims that reviewers see as promising but not yet fully realized.
